results.text:
Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

“I don’t know whether I want something serious with you. I’m not pretending I do. I’d still like to have sex.”

That may be candid about what you expect now. It doesn’t settle what either of you will owe if the act creates something neither of you expected. Sex can make a child. If this girl gets pregnant, she’s gonna call you. Then what? You block her? Agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort when she thinks abortion is killing her child? This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.

The STI part is easy: say what you know, or say you don’t know. Feelings aren’t. You can both mean it when you say this is only sex and still have one of you get attached afterward. If you’re both really numb or robotic about sex, maybe not.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. You have to care what happens to the person afterward. Otherwise you’re using and abusing them for pleasure. Maybe they’re using you too. Congratulations, now it’s mutual.

A lot of “I only want fun” really means, “This is the only version of the relationship that gets me laid.” Sometimes I know I’m hoping it turns into love. Sometimes I only find out I was hoping that when it doesn’t.

And then there’s the situationship, which is hard to define because that’s basically the point. Usually it’s a happenstance relationship based on sex. There’s less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. You’re regularly having sex, going out together, spending time alone together, and doing things you wouldn’t do with a regular friend. It feels like it’s filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally—maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

It can go either way. Often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy. Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. Refusing to name the relationship doesn’t make the responsibility disappear. What they don’t escape is the existential void created by another superficial fix. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

And “Why are you making this heavy?” can be a real question. They may actually mean: don’t you want the fun, and are you about to give it up? My answer would be: I’m trying to understand whether this is really fulfilling me or if it’s drainingly superficial.

I had something sort of like that with H., although ours was much deeper than what people normally mean by situationship. We were BFFs and spent nearly all our time together. She was falling in love with me, and I wasn’t falling in love with her. She felt more like a sister to me, partly because I’m not attracted to white women. Ours wasn’t superficial. It was just painfully uneven.

But here's the funny thing many people don't understand: labels don't create commitment. They can still expose whether two people think they're in the same relationship, which matters a lot.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label. If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me; I don't need a promise on paper to make me want to. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that's a red flag.

In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. If anybody was supposed to be winning that arrangement, it was him. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

results.text:
Are you ready for the crucible?

I call relationship a crucible because I was thinking of Dr. David Schnarch’s Crucible Approach in Passionate Marriage. Schnarch saw marriage as a natural “people-growing process.” His idea of differentiation was learning to hold onto yourself while staying close, especially when intimacy brings anxiety and unresolved problems to the surface.

That’s definitely what relationship has done to me.

One warning before I romanticize the crucible too much: sometimes this isn't two wounded people triggering each other but one person terrorizing or controlling the other. If you're scared to say no or tell the truth, or scared of what happens if you leave, don't treat that as a mutual communication exercise—get other people involved and think about safety first.

Toft says meditation, yoga, prayer, and church are all fine, but after fifty years of marriage his main spiritual practice is being in relationship with his wife. I understand what he means. It’s much easier for me to feel spiritually advanced when nobody is close enough to expose the parts of me that aren’t.

Being in a relationship showed me how vulnerable I actually am when I open my heart. It’s really easy to feel invulnerable and strong when you’re alone, or even just with friends. Taking off the masks and showing your inner child is a gamble, but it’s required if you want to go deeper in yourself and deeper with another person.

Living alone is easy in so many ways. I can make my bed whenever I want. When I have a girlfriend, making the bed in the morning can become one of the ways I show her I love her. If I don’t do it well, somehow it may become a bad omen that I don’t care about her.

A tiny thing can end up carrying way more emotional weight than it should.

Dealing with somebody else’s emotional insecurities can also be exhausting. It’s easy to feel free when I don’t have to do that. I actually don’t have that much skill with people, and this works fine until I’m in a romantic relationship and suddenly I’m expected to mind-read, notice every emotional shift, check in constantly, and understand what a silence means.

Relationship may activate wounds that were already there. Sometimes it may open a level of the heart that is simply very young and vulnerable, whether you knew there was a wound there or not. You become like a baby again. There’s a reason lovers call each other “baby” and “my baby.”

That can be an incredible therapy opportunity. Every such opportunity also carries a risk of failure and more trauma.

With Bee, Key, and H.D., there was always some sense that they were remembering how their dad treated them and judging me according to how close to him—or different from him—I was. That puts me in a tough position. I want to play the role they need in some way, but I don’t want to leave the reality of me being me.

A smaller example happened with all of them. They could message me whenever they wanted, even a day later. If I took a day to respond, suddenly it was weird. What was I doing? What did it mean?

The present issue may be tiny. The part reacting to it may be five years old.

Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship. My standards used to be very low and now they are much higher because I’m exhausted by drama. Other people will have different standards above that minimum.

At the very least, there needs to be honesty, real effort at improving, and some ability to stop blaming everybody else for your own problems.

Inner-child reparenting is a big part of this. The present-day adult has to learn how to parent the child part instead of quietly hiring the partner for the job.

It can get pretty entitled when you expect your partner to know what you need without being told. You may barely see your own pattern, and then deny it instead of taking responsibility when they point it out.

Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.

A peer can give another angle. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.

That’s why I recommend peer counseling outside the couple. If my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don’t understand it.

I also have to deal with what happens in my body. My mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her. Meanwhile my body feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow. It becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on. That is another reason to have a peer counselor.

Breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or the Buteyko method is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that. Other times it’s hard to tell. I explain more of the body-based options in my Somatic Modalities guide.

Somatic Modalities Strategic Sequencing Roadmap

Meditation matters a lot to me too. For most people I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet. Meditation is also an easy road into spiritual bypassing, so it is a double-edged sword.
